title: Brandenburg Concerto No. 3 in G major
hook: Three violins, three violas, three cellos and no soloist: everyone is the soloist in turn.

painting.title: The Little Concert (Il concertino)
painting.pairingNote: Three string players crowd round one table of music in a Venetian drawing room, two decades after Bach’s concerto for strings in groups of three.

facts: In 1721 Bach, then music director to Prince Leopold at Köthen, copied out six concertos in his own hand and sent them to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, with a dedication in French dated 24 March. He called them *Six concertos for several instruments*; the name “Brandenburg” came later.

No. 3 is written for strings only, in three equal groups: three violins, three violas and three cellos, with a bass line and harpsichord, the [[continuo|continuo]], underneath. There is no soloist. The nine players form three teams of three, and any of them may step forward with the tune for a moment.

The middle movement is famous for being almost empty: Bach wrote one bar with two slow chords. He probably expected a player to improvise something before or around them, a short [[cadenza|cadenza]]. Every ensemble fills the gap in its own way.

Bach later reused the first movement, with added oboes and horns, as the opening Sinfonia of his cantata *Ich liebe den Höchsten von ganzem Gemüte*, BWV 174 (1729). The concerto is the shortest of the six.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a busy, cheerful game of teams (I), a pause on two chords (II), a whirling dance (III).

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: Bach gave this movement no tempo marking; it is always played at a brisk pace. A bright refrain for everyone, the [[ritornello|ritornello]], is built from a three-note figure that bounces between two notes. Between its returns the three teams toss short figures back and forth, and the texture keeps changing from a solid mass of strings to a web of nine separate parts.

mainIdeas.name: The bouncing figure
mainIdeas.description: three quick notes, up and back, repeated and passed around.

mainIdeas.name: The exchanges
mainIdeas.description: one group plays a figure, another answers, a third joins in.

notice: Listen for the cellos. In most Baroque music they only play the bass; here they get the tune in their turn.
Notice how often the bouncing three-note figure appears, high and low, in every group.

movements.heading: Adagio
movements.summary: In Bach’s score the slow movement is one bar: two chords, the second leaving the music hanging, so that the finale follows as an answer. In this recording Trevor Pinnock fills the gap with a short slow movement Bach wrote for an early version of his Sonata in G for violin and harpsichord (BWV 1019a), ending on the same kind of open chord.

mainIdeas.name: The two chords
mainIdeas.description: a quiet, questioning close that leads straight into the finale.

stops.hear: Slow, quiet, searching music, very short
stops.happening: Pinnock’s choice of a few bars from another Bach work, played where Bach left space

stops.label: Last 5 seconds
stops.hear: A chord that sounds unfinished, like a question
stops.happening: The two chords of Bach’s score, a half close in E minor

notice: Listen to how the last chord does not settle. The finale, which follows at once, is the answer.

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: A fast, whirling dance in groups of three notes, close to a jig. It starts with the violins and spreads through the whole band. The movement has two parts, the second much longer than the first, and each is played twice.

mainIdeas.name: The whirl
mainIdeas.description: quick notes in threes, rushing up and down the scale, passed from group to group.

stops.hear: A rush of quick notes in the violins, taken up at once by the others
The figure sets off again, passed between the groups and through new keys
The music passes through minor keys before heading home

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The English Concert play on period instruments with a small string group; the album credits list a first, second and third viola and cello, as in Bach’s score. Trevor Pinnock directs from the harpsichord. The recording was made in Henry Wood Hall in London in 1982.

threads.title: Strength in threes
threads.body: Three violins, three violas, three cellos; the opening figure is three notes; the finale moves in groups of three; there are three movements.

threads.title: Everyone a soloist
threads.body: In a Baroque concerto a small group of soloists usually stands out from the band. Here the band is the soloist: every part takes the lead at some point.

threads.title: The empty middle
threads.body: A whole movement of one bar, two chords long. Bach leaves it open, and each performance answers the question differently.
